strengths: Clear problem motivation: identifies genuine limitation of 3DGS under large FoV and non-perspective cameras
Mathematically rigorous development with elegant closed-form ray-Gaussian integral solution in canonical coordinate space
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, Aria, MipNeRF360) with consistent improvements of 2-4.8 PSNR on wide-FoV
Thorough baseline comparisons (3DGS, FisheyeGS, EVER, 3DGUT) and extensive evaluation metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS)
Good generalization to unseen camera FoVs and practical runtime performance comparable to 3DGS
Well-documented implementation with detailed appendices, reproducibility statement, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: ray-Gaussian integration via canonical coordinates is mathematically elegant but relatively straightforward; PBF is standard frustum computation; BEAP is incremental projection representation
Incremental contribution relative to growing literature on wide-FoV Gaussians (EVER, 3DGUT, FisheyeGS, 2DGS, HTGS); builds on rather than fundamentally reconceptualizes existing approaches
Central claim of 'exactness' is overstated: Appendix A acknowledges inability to fully resolve self-occlusion and ordering, undermining key motivation

Insufficient ablation studies: no clear decomposition showing which component (ray formulation, PBF, BEAP) drives improvements; limited justification for why ray-based approach is superior to prior alternatives

Experimental concerns: marginal runtime improvements (~0.14ms), modest cross-camera generalization gains, unclear if baselines received equal optimization effort, and Fig. 8 showing split-based methods partially close the gap
Limited practical scope: improvements most significant for niche applications (extreme fisheye, robotics); most test scenes are indoor/moderate complexity; method requires 'reasonably-scaled' scenes
Presentation could better explain intuitions earlier; insufficient discussion of when geometric exactness matters versus where standard 3DGS suffices; relationship to 2DGS and HTGS unclear
Complex PBF solver with multiple heuristics (λ parameter, mirror angle transformations in D.2) lack rigorous justification and sensitivity analysis
Numerical stability issues (Section C.7) relegated to brief treatment despite importance; concern about subtle implementation errors given complex derivations

strengths: Mathematically rigorous derivation of exact ray-Gaussian integral for generic camera models, replacing linear approximations in prior work
Well-integrated technical framework combining exact rendering, efficient PBF association, and unified BEAP supervision
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, MipNeRF360, etc.) with proper protocols and extensive ablations
Strong generalization across camera types and impressive 5-8× speedup over ray-tracing methods on wide-FoV benchmarks
Addresses practical and underexplored problem of wide-FoV and generic camera support in Gaussian splatting
Excellent reproducibility with detailed mathematical appendices, implementation details, and promised code release
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of geometric concepts and comprehensive supplementary materials
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty - exact ray-Gaussian integral is mathematically straightforward once properly formulated; PBF and BEAP are primarily engineering contributions
Modest practical improvements on standard pinhole cameras (Tab. 2: 0.3-0.5 PSNR gains), with significant benefits mainly for specialized wide-FoV scenarios
Incomplete handling of acknowledged limitations (self-occlusion, ordering still rely on depth sorting); 'exactness' claim is relative to splitting-based approximation only

Narrow application scope - improvements most significant for wide-FoV cameras which represent smaller fraction of practical use cases; limited demonstration of robotics/autonomous driving applications
Limited experimental scope - all experiments on images ≤1080p without scalability analysis; missing comparisons with some recent 2024-2025 methods on standard benchmarks
Insufficient analysis of when exactness provides practical benefit - no error bounds or quantitative comparison showing conditions where exact rendering significantly outperforms approximations
No direct ablation isolating 'exactness' contribution from PBF efficiency gains; Section 4.4 comparison is somewhat indirect
